At a glance

Best months
  • March for the Varanger seaduck with enough light to work in
  • June into early July for the seabird cliffs, the breeding tundra and the midnight sun
Getting around
Fly to Kirkenes for Varanger and Pasvik, and hire a car. Winter driving needs studded tyres, and covering the length of the country means internal flights
The one thing to know
Norway is genuinely expensive and the far north adds internal flights on top, so the budget wants settling before the itinerary does

When to Go

The Norwegian year is decided by light. Varanger in winter is dark and holds the eider flocks, Varanger in June has no night at all and the cliffs are full. Those are two different trips to the same place.

winter

November to March

The eider season, and the reason Varanger has a winter trade at all. Polar night through midwinter, with the light returning fast from February.

Go for Steller's Eider, King Eider, Gyrfalcon and the auks returning to Hornøya.

Trade off Studded tyres, very short days in December and January, and genuine cold.

Typical daily average
  • Vardø: -6 to -1 °C / 21 to 30 °F
  • Bodø: -3 to 2 °C / 27 to 36 °F
  • Ålesund: 1 to 5 °C / 34 to 41 °F

spring

April to May

The changeover. Seabird cliffs fill, the taiga owls start calling and the tundra waders arrive as the snow leaves.

Go for Owls in Pasvik, seabirds returning, the first tundra breeders.

Trade off Roads on the plateau can still be closed, and the taiga is between seasons.

Typical daily average
  • Vardø: -1 to 3 °C / 30 to 37 °F
  • Bodø: 2 to 8 °C / 36 to 46 °F
  • Ålesund: 4 to 9 °C / 39 to 48 °F

summer

June to July

Midnight sun, and no night at all in Finnmark. Every colony is occupied and the tundra is breeding, which makes this the fullest list of the year.

Go for Hornøya at its fullest, tundra waders and skuas, Runde's puffins, the mountain plateaus.

Trade off Mosquitoes in the taiga are serious, and Norwegian prices are at their highest.

Typical daily average
  • Vardø: 6 to 10 °C / 43 to 50 °F
  • Bodø: 9 to 15 °C / 48 to 59 °F
  • Ålesund: 10 to 15 °C / 50 to 59 °F

autumn

August to October

Colonies empty and passage runs down the coast, with the light shortening quickly through September.

Go for Wader and seabird passage, White-tailed Eagle throughout.

Trade off The seabird cliffs are over by late August and the weather turns early.

Typical daily average
  • Vardø: 4 to 8 °C / 39 to 46 °F
  • Bodø: 7 to 11 °C / 45 to 52 °F
  • Ålesund: 8 to 13 °C / 46 to 55 °F

Varanger

An Arctic fjord that stays ice free all winter, with a seabird island you walk onto and open tundra behind

Varanger is the reason birders come to Norway, and it carries most of the trade. Steller's Eider and King Eider winter in the fjord in numbers, Hornøya off Vardø is a seabird cliff you can walk onto with Brünnich's Guillemot on it, and the tundra behind holds Gyrfalcon and Rough-legged Buzzard.

  • Habitat: A fifty-metre cliff falling into the Barents Sea at Store Ekkerøy with 10,000 Kittiwakes on its ledges, heather moor behind, and the shallow fjord below Nesseby.
  • When: Seabirds return to the cliffs from March and passerines arrive in May, and most have gone again between mid-August and mid-September. The fjord winters 10,000 to 20,000 Steller's Eiders.
  • Getting there: The E75 runs the length of the fjord from Varangerbotn to Vardø. Store Ekkerøy is a signed turning east of Vadsø, and the Hornøya boat leaves Vardø harbour.
  • Look for: Steller's Eider, King Eider, Thick-billed Murre, Gyrfalcon, Rough-legged Buzzard, Atlantic Puffin, Common Eider, Yellow-billed Loon
  • Parks and reserves: Varangerhalvøya National Park, Ekkerøy Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : A seabird island twenty minutes by boat from Vardø, with a path up through the colony. It is the one place in Europe a Brünnich's Guillemot is at arm's length.
    • : The harbour town at the fjord's mouth. It is the base for the island boat, and King Eider flocks winter in the harbour itself.
    • : A headland of nesting Kittiwakes, with a road to the foot of the cliff. The shore below it fills with waders on the tide.
    • : The fjord's main town. Steller's Eider sit offshore through the winter, and most visitors fly into the airstrip here.
    • : A small fishing settlement on the outer coast. Search it for divers, Long-tailed Duck and the passage skuas.
    • : The road end on the treeless outer coast, an hour beyond Vardø. It is the emptiest place on the peninsula.
    • : A working fishing port whose gutting waste holds gull flocks all winter. Its harbour is where a King Eider is most reliably seen.
  • Also covers: Ekkerøy Nature Reserve, Hamningberg, Hornøya, Kiberg, Kongsfjord, Vadsø, Varangerhalvøya National Park, Vardø
  • Also watch for: Killer Whale and Humpback Whale follow herring into the fjords through the winter. Reindeer are herded across the whole peninsula and Arctic Fox holds a small monitored population on the tundra behind Batsfjord.

Pasvik and the border taiga

The only true Siberian taiga in the country, running south from Kirkenes along the Russian frontier

The Pasvik valley runs south from Kirkenes along the Russian border, and it is the only piece of true Siberian taiga in the country. Great Grey Owl, Northern Hawk-Owl, Siberian Jay, Pine Grosbeak and Eurasian Three-toed Woodpecker all hold territory in the old pine forest along it.

  • Habitat: The one arm of true Siberian taiga in Norway, old pine over bog and lake, pressed against the Russian border along the Pasvik river.
  • When: June and early July, when the taiga species are in song and the road is reliably open. Winter closes most of the valley to anything but a snowmobile.
  • Getting there: The 885 runs south from Kirkenes down the whole valley to Vaggatem and the national park. Kirkenes has the airport and is the only town of any size.
  • Look for: Great Grey Owl, Northern Hawk-Owl, Siberian Jay, Pine Grosbeak, Eurasian Three-toed Woodpecker, Rustic Bunting, Western Capercaillie
  • National park:
    • Øvre Pasvik National Park, The largest stand of natural Siberian pine taiga in Norway, on the Russian border. It holds Siberian Jay, Siberian Tit and Pine Grosbeak.
  • Stops:
    • : The wetland reserve along the river. A tower at Fjærvann looks over cranes, divers and the Bean Geese that breed in the bog behind.
    • : The town at the head of the fjord and the base for the whole valley. It has an airport and the last supermarket before the border road.
  • Also covers: Kirkenes, Øvre Pasvik National Park, Pasvik Nature Reserve, Treriksrøysa tripoint
  • Also watch for: Brown Bear, Elk and Beaver all use the Pasvik valley, and the Norwegian side carries one of the densest brown bear populations in the country. Wolverine ranges the fells above.

The Tana river tundra

The largest salmon valley in the north, with the Finnmarksvidda plateau of open tundra above it

Bluethroat, Lapland Bunting, Red-necked Phalarope and Long-tailed Skua are on the approach roads through the summer, which is the season the ground is reachable at all.

  • Habitat: A 3,450 ha delta of shallow water and sandbank where the Tana meets its fjord, flooded at high tide, with a grass islet offshore and scrub on the river banks.
  • When: Early May to July for the breeding ducks and waders. Huge moulting flocks gather from early August, and winter holds 4,000 Eiders, 4,000 Long-tailed Ducks and 800 King Eiders.
  • Getting there: The E6 crosses the river at Tana bru and the 98 follows the eastern bank north to Leirpollen, from where the delta and the tidal flats are scanned.
  • Look for: Bluethroat, Lapland Longspur, Red-necked Phalarope, Long-tailed Jaeger, Temminck's Stint, Arctic Warbler, Little Bunting
  • Parks and reserves: Tanamunningen Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : The bridge town where the road crosses the Tana. The river valley is watched from here in both directions.
    • : A village on the Tana forty kilometres upriver. The birch and willow banks of the largest salmon river in northern Europe hold Bluethroat, Redpoll and Rustic Bunting.
    • : The open mountain plateau the road crosses between Tana and Laksefjord. The Long-tailed Skua and the Dotterel are here.
  • Also covers: Finnmarksvidda approach roads, Ifjord, Finnmark, Polmak, Tana Bru, Tana river / Teno river valley, Tanamunningen Nature Reserve
  • Also watch for: Reindeer are herded across the whole of the Finnmarksvidda and cross the roads constantly in summer. Elk use the river woodland, and Arctic Fox and Wolverine hold the open plateau.

Lofoten and Vesterålen

A wall of mountains straight out of the sea, with seabird colonies on the outer islands and a whale port at Andenes

White-tailed Eagle are throughout the chain, and the outer islands carry the seabird colonies. Andenes on Andøya is the departure point for whales and seabirds together.

  • Habitat: An archipelago of 1,277 km² of granite peaks rising straight out of the sea, with seabird cliffs on the outer islands of Røst and Værøy and marsh on Røstlandet.
  • When: May to August, when the weather is at its best and the breeding seabirds are in. March and April, and September to November, both carry seabird movement.
  • Getting there: The E10 runs the chain from Fiskebøl to Å. The Røst and Værøy cliffs need a boat, and access to them is closed from 15 April to 15 August.
  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, European Shag, Black Guillemot, Northern Fulmar, Black-legged Kittiwake, Common Murre, Purple Sandpiper
  • National park: Møysalen National Park
  • Stops:
    • : The town at the northern tip of Andøya. The whale boats leave from it, and the shore carries White-tailed Eagle and eider all year.
    • : The postcard village under the Lofoten wall. It is the base for the Værøy and Røst boats out to the puffin colonies.
    • : The ferry port at the end of the island chain. Search it for shearwater and skua passage on an onshore wind.
    • : The blanket bog and shallow lagoon reserve on Andøya's west coast. Whimbrel, Golden Plover and Red-necked Phalarope breed here.
  • Also covers: Andenes, Andøya, Leknes wetlands, Moskenes, Møysalen National Park, Reine, Skogvoll
  • Also watch for: Andenes is the departure point for Sperm Whale, which feed year round in the deep canyon just offshore, with Orca and Humpback Whale following the winter herring. Eurasian Otter is common along the shoreline.

Runde and the seabird cliffs

The southernmost large seabird colony in the country and the easiest to reach, connected to the mainland by road

Runde is the southernmost large seabird colony in Norway and the most accessible, and a road runs to it from Ålesund. Puffin, Gannet, Kittiwake and Fulmar nest on the Goksøyr cliffs, and a research centre sits on the island.

  • Habitat: A small island 70 km south of Ålesund, bridged to its neighbours, whose seabird colonies are nature reserves that can be watched from the paths outside them.
  • When: April to August, and May or June for the colonies at their most active. Migrants pass in good numbers, and a few seabirds linger on the sea through winter.
  • Getting there: Take the E39 south from Ålesund, then the 654 through Fosnavåg and over the bridge to Runde. The path to the cliffs starts from the car park above the village.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Atlantic Puffin, Razorbill, European Storm Petrel, Great Cormorant, Common Eider, Great Skua
  • Parks and reserves: Runde Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : An island of half a million seabirds. A road bridge reaches it, and a marked path climbs onto the cliff top above the Puffin and Gannet colonies.
    • : The hamlet the cliff path starts from, and the shortest walk to the colony viewpoints.
    • : The art nouveau town an hour inland of the island. It is the practical base and airport for it.
  • Also covers: Ålesund, Goksøyr cliffs, Runde Environmental Centre, Runde island, Runde Nature Reserve
  • Also watch for: Grey Seal and Harbour Seal both haul out below the Goksoyr cliffs, and Eurasian Otter works the island shoreline at dawn.

Smøla and the White-tailed Eagle coast

A low island of bare rock and lochans holding one of the densest White-tailed Eagle populations anywhere

Smøla lies off the Trøndelag coast, and its wind farm is the best studied case in the world of what turbines do to eagles.

  • Habitat: Several hundred islands and islets around a partly cultivated main island, otherwise a mosaic of open mire, coastal heath and shallow water, one of Norway's largest marine wetlands.
  • When: Late autumn to early spring is the season here. Waders arrive in numbers from September, seaduck and divers build through October, and early March can be outstanding.
  • Getting there: The ferry runs from Edøya, on the coast road from Kristiansund. The island roads are quiet, and the shallow bays are watched from lay-bys along them.
  • Look for: Red-throated Loon, Black-throated Loon, Common Snipe, Eurasian Curlew, Willow Ptarmigan, Common Redshank, Arctic Tern
  • Parks and reserves: Smøla Archipelago Protected Landscape
  • Stops:
    • : A low archipelago of ten thousand islets, on a ferry from Edøya. It carries one of the densest White-tailed Eagle populations in the world.
    • : The island's main settlement and harbour. The eagle safari boats leave from here.
    • : The mainland town the ferry runs from, with an airport and the coastal road south.
  • Also covers: Hopen, Kristiansund, Smøla Archipelago Protected Landscape, Smøla island, Smøla wind farm area
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Otter is common on the island shoreline, and Harbour Seal and Grey Seal use the outer skerries. Red Deer swim between the islands.

Dovrefjell and the high plateau

High plateau in the middle of the country under the Snohetta massif, shared with a musk ox herd

Gyrfalcon, Dotterel, Long-tailed Skua and Ptarmigan work the fell under Snøhetta, and a musk ox herd shares the same ground.

  • Habitat: High mountain plateau above the tree line, with the Fokstumyra mire complex of 7.5 km² of pools, creeks and birch and willow scrub on its northern edge.
  • When: Late May to July and no other season: the climate is severe and the birds are scarce outside it. June and July are the two months at Fokstumyra.
  • Getting there: Dombås is 10 km south and sits on the E6 and the Oslo to Trondheim railway. Access is restricted in the breeding season to one marked trail from Fokstua, so stay on it.
  • Look for: Eurasian Dotterel, Rock Ptarmigan, Snow Bunting, Snowy Owl, Ring Ouzel, Golden Eagle, European Golden Plover
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Dovrefjell-Sunndalsfjella National Park, High tundra plateau above the treeline. It is the southernmost breeding ground for several arctic birds, and it is why the mountain species are reachable by train.
    • Fokstumyra Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : A mountain station on the railway, with a botanical garden behind it. It is the standard base for the Snøhetta walk.
    • : The old military station on the plateau. Open ground either side of the road carries Dotterel, Shore Lark and Long-tailed Skua.
    • : The plateau's highest ground at 2,286 m. Walk it from Kongsvold for Ptarmigan, Snow Bunting and the musk ox herd.
  • Also covers: Dovrefjell-Sunndalsfjella National Park, Fokstumyra Nature Reserve, Hjerkinn, Kongsvold, Snøhetta massif
  • Also watch for: Musk Ox were reintroduced from Greenland in the 1930s and around three hundred now range the plateau. Guided walks from Hjerkinn are how they are watched. Wild Reindeer hold Europe's last genuinely wild herd here, with Wolverine and Arctic Fox on the same ground.

Hardangervidda and Bjoreidalen

The largest mountain plateau in northern Europe, treeless above 1,000 m and crossed by one road

Hardangervidda covers more than 5,000 km² between 1,000 and 1,500 m, and 3,430 km² of it is the largest national park on the Norwegian mainland. The plateau is the southwestern edge of the European breeding range for a set of Arctic birds, so Eurasian Dotterel, Long-tailed Jaeger, Temminck's Stint and Purple Sandpiper all breed within sight of road 7. Bjoreidalen, the mountain wetland on the northern rim, holds at least twelve breeding wader species on its own.

  • Habitat: A treeless plateau between 1,000 and 1,500 m covered in lakes, mires and low heath, with a mountain river valley and willow scrub at Bjoreidalen on its northern edge.
  • When: Late May and June where the snow has gone, and the first half of July once the whole plateau opens. Late August and September bring migrants and the reindeer hunt.
  • Getting there: Road 7 crosses the northern plateau between Geilo and Eidfjord and is the main way in. Park at the Dyranut lodge on that road for the marked trail into Bjoreidalen. The toll road to Tinnhølen opens in the last days of June. The Bergen railway serves Finse and Haugastøl, and Finse has no road, so the train is the only approach to it.
  • Look for: Eurasian Dotterel, Rock Ptarmigan, Willow Ptarmigan, Long-tailed Jaeger, Temminck's Stint, Purple Sandpiper, Red-necked Phalarope, Horned Lark, Lapland Longspur, Snow Bunting, Great Snipe
  • Stops:
    • : A treeless plateau scattered with lakes and mires. Road 7 crosses its northern edge, which is where most of the birding is done, and walking out from the road opens the rest of it.
    • : A mountain wetland of river, shore scrub and open plain on the northern rim. At least twelve wader species breed, and the reserve stays closed to visitors until 15 June.
    • : A station at 1,222 m on the Bergen railway with no road to it. The ground around it is high and close to the glacier, and walking south from it reaches the plateau.
    • : A station on the same line at the eastern edge of the plateau. Buses run west from here, which puts the vidda in reach without a car.
    • : The town on the northeastern approach and the usual base. The road from here towards Uvdal is a standard starting point for excursions onto the high ground.
  • Also covers: Bjoreidalen, Finse, Geilo, Hardangervidda National Park, Haugastøl
  • Also watch for: Hardangervidda holds the largest herd of wild Reindeer in Europe, with 10,000 to 12,000 animals on the plateau in winter. Arctic Fox and Norwegian Lemming are both here, and a lemming year lifts every predator on the plateau.

Utsira and the Jæren coast

The Norwegian rarity island, and the long sand coast and lowland lakes below Stavanger

Utsira is 6 km² of rock, heath and shelter belt 25 km out from Haugesund, and the gardens in its one farmed valley are the only cover for miles, so migrants pile into them. A good fall drops hundreds of Bluethroats and Common Redstarts on the island, Yellow-browed Warbler and Barred Warbler are annual, and an autumn count from the shore has reached 35,000 Northern Fulmars in a day. South of Stavanger, Jærstrendene carries the largest dunes and sand beaches in Norway, with Orrevatnet and Grudavatnet behind them.

  • Habitat: A small rocky island of heath, outcrop and sheltered garden 25 km offshore, with the mainland coast opposite carrying the largest sand beaches and dune fields in Norway and a chain of shallow lowland lakes behind them.
  • When: April and May, and September and October, when the passerine falls and the seabird passage both peak. June, July and the winter months are quiet by comparison.
  • Getting there: Utsira is reached by boat from Haugesund, with daily sailings, and some departures leave from Karmøy. The Jæren sites lie along road 44 and road 510 south of Stavanger, and most of them are within half an hour of the city.
  • Look for: Northern Fulmar, Manx Shearwater, Sooty Shearwater, Atlantic Puffin, European Shag, Yellow-browed Warbler, Barred Warbler, Richard's Pipit, Common Rosefinch, Purple Sandpiper
  • Stops:
    • : A small rocky island with one farmed valley, a few conifer plantations and a set of well kept gardens. The boat from Haugesund takes an hour, and the whole island can be covered in a day on foot or by bicycle.
    • : Sixteen square kilometres of beach, dune and shallow water south of Stavanger, and the largest sand coast in Norway. Divers, sea duck, waders and auks pass offshore through April and May and again from August to October.
    • : The headland and bird observatory in the middle of the Jæren beaches. It stands metres from Orrevatnet, which makes it the one stop that covers both the sea and the lake.
    • : A shallow lake behind the dunes and the most important bird lake in Norway. Great Crested Grebe, Pied Avocet and Black-tailed Godwit breed, and Whooper Swan arrives late in the year and stays.
    • : Two shallow lakes joined by a stream, with an observation tower at the edge of the reserve. The tower is as close as visitors may go and it covers the whole of the water.
    • : The southern end of the beach strip, with an old lighthouse station and a visitor point on the shore. It is the quietest of the recommended stretches in summer.
  • Also covers: Borestranden and the Jæren beaches, Grudavatnet, Haugesund, Jærstrendene, Kvassheim, Orrevatnet, Revtangen, Utsira
  • Also watch for: Harbour Porpoise and Grey Seal are both regular in the sound between Utsira and the mainland, and Harbour Seal hauls out on the skerries at the northern end of Jærstrendene.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Norway?

It depends which trip you want, and the two are opposites. March for the Varanger seaduck, when the eider flocks are still in and there is enough light to work. June and early July for everything else, when the seabird cliffs are full and the tundra is breeding under a midnight sun.

Where do I see Steller's Eider?

Varanger, and Båtsfjord harbour in particular, where the flock sits close enough to watch from the quay. The birds breed in the Russian Arctic and winter on this one Norwegian fjord.

What is special about Hornøya?

It is a seabird cliff you can walk onto. A boat runs from Vardø and puts you ashore among breeding Brünnich's Guillemot, Common Guillemot, Razorbill, Kittiwake and Puffin, which is a rare thing anywhere.

Is Svalbard part of a Norway birding trip?

It is sold both ways. Some operators fold it into a Norwegian itinerary and others sell it as its own Arctic voyage, and both patterns are current. Treat it as a separate decision from the mainland.

How expensive is Norway?

Genuinely expensive, and it is worth budgeting for before committing. Accommodation, fuel and food all run well above western European levels, and the far north adds internal flights on top.

Do I need a car?

Yes, and in winter it needs studded tyres. The Varanger road runs out along the fjord through every site on the trip, and there is no practical alternative to driving it.

What certification should I look for in Norwegian accommodation?

Miljøfyrtårn, the Eco-Lighthouse, which is the national scheme and describes itself as the country's most used certificate. Green Key carries few Norwegian properties, so it is the wrong thing to look for.

Who are the birding institutions in Norway?

BirdLife Norge is the membership organisation and runs the rarities committee. The Environment Agency and the national park boards manage the reserves, and Biotope in Vardø is an architecture practice that designs birding hides along the Varanger coast.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Norway has 18 local bird clubs across 18 regions. See every Norwegian club by region.

BirdLife Norge The national membership organisation, formerly Norsk Ornitologisk Forening. It runs the rarities committee and the monitoring. Visit Biotope An architecture practice based in Vardø that designs and builds birding hides and shelters along the Varanger coast. There is nothing else like it in Europe. Visit Miljodirektoratet The Norwegian Environment Agency, which sits above the county governors who manage the reserves above. Visit Runde Environmental Centre A research and visitor centre on Runde island, and the practical base for the southernmost large seabird colony in the country. Visit
